title: Routines: in the beginning and beyond
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino extends the familiar case for classroom routines by asking two less-considered questions: what should become routine, and what happens next. Drawing on Peps Mccrea and James Dyke, she separates instructional routines from behavioural ones and lists the sixteen or so actions, from entry to exit, that a teacher might make routine to free working memory for learning. She rejects the objection that routines stifle creativity, arguing there is joy in knowing things. Her central story is a cover lesson in which a supposedly established routine collapsed because the cue phrase had no shared meaning beyond her own classroom. The fix is to make the purpose explicit each time, pass cues and procedures to cover teachers, and aim for routines that run independently of the teacher.
points: Decide what to routinise by distinguishing instructional routines (things done often) from behavioural routines (actions at each lesson stage).
Rare actions need simple, quick routines, because complicated ones demand many repetitions to embed.
Routines that lapse increase cognitive load and lost time, so entry and exit cues and the procedure must be explicit and consistent.
A routine that depends on the teacher present is not established; explaining the purpose each time and briefing cover staff builds independence.
Routines are defended as the means to joy and learning, not a rigidity that stifles it.
quotes: Routines are key to a classroom conducive to learning. Peps Mccrea perfectly explains the power of a good routine in his book, Motivated Teaching, and summarises it in this tweet: These are significant gains. It takes time and commitment from both teachers and students to successfully embed good routines.

Behavioural routines encompass the actions of teachers and students during each stage of the lesson. If you regularly collect in and hand out books, then having a routine for this is necessary to make the process time-efficient and freeing up working memory space for learning instead.
To ensure the focus of your lesson is on the learning, every action should become routine. - How do students enter?
Some people may argue that this type of management limits creativity and brings in a rigidity that stifles joy. On the contrary, there is so much joy in knowing things.
If there is any lapse in establishing routines, then they do the opposite and increase cognitive load and time lost in lessons (Leinhardt et al., 1987).

When I start the routine, I say ‘time for independent working’. As it is not a universally utilised phrase that has a shared meaning throughout the school, it may not mean the same thing to students when a different teacher uses the phrase in my lesson.
The routine then fades into the background, automating important actions and behaviours, eventually allowing the focus to be solely on the learning. Bliss.
